summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes  
- **Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2226(h) (Adrian's Law)** — the investigating agency shall visually observe the child who is the alleged victim; in a joint investigation DCF and law enforcement shall both observe the child, and DCF policy states that law enforcement's observation does not fulfill DCF's responsibility (DCF PPM 2010)  
- **Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2226(b)** — a joint DCF / law enforcement investigation is mandatory when a report indicates serious physical harm to, serious deterioration of, or sexual abuse of the child and action may be required to protect the child (DCF PPM 1530)

regulations_applicable.title: Agency 30 - KANSAS DEPARTMENT FOR CHILDREN AND FAMILIES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed the CINC adjudication and the termination of parental rights, holding that ICWA's 'qualified expert witness' requirement demands expertise beyond ordinary social-worker credentials, that Kansas courts should consult the ICWA legislative history and the BIA Guidelines, and that the absence of such testimony is not harmless error.
key_cases.relevance: Once ICWA applies to a Kansas child, the State must produce a witness with tribal or Indian child-welfare expertise before the child can be placed in foster care or rights terminated.
key_cases.quote: the ICWA heightens the requirements for an expert's qualifications beyond those normally required in a proceeding governed solely by state statutes

key_cases.holding: Reviewing a collateral order, the court held that a non-Indian biological mother's preference for a non-Indian adoptive family is not, absent a request for anonymity, good cause to deviate from ICWA's placement preferences, and reversed the district court's good-cause finding.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Kansas statement of how 25 U.S.C. § 1915 placement preferences bind state courts once a child is an 'Indian child,' regardless of the parent's own wishes.
key_cases.quote: absent a request for anonymity by a biological parent, a parent's placement preference cannot override ICWA's placement factors

key_cases.holding: The court overruled In re Adoption of Baby Boy L. and abandoned the judicially created 'existing Indian family' doctrine, holding that ICWA applies to a child of both Indian and non-Indian heritage without any threshold inquiry into the family's cultural connection to the tribe.
key_cases.relevance: Kansas no longer screens out ICWA cases by asking whether the child came from an 'existing Indian family,' so ICWA attaches whenever the statutory definition of Indian child is met.
key_cases.quote: we hereby overrule Baby Boy L., 231 Kan. 199, and abandon its existing Indian family doctrine

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court rejected all challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's authority to enact it, reversing on the anticommandeering claims, and vacating for lack of standing the equal protection and nondelegation challenges to the placement preferences.
key_cases.relevance: ICWA remains fully enforceable against Kansas courts and agencies, including its notice, active efforts, expert witness and placement preference requirements.
key_cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding that ordering a parent to undergo a clinical or substance abuse evaluation in a CINC case does not violate the Fifth Amendment, that non-compliance may be considered in the unfitness analysis, and that a parent's demonstrated unwillingness to participate in treatment may be weighed in deciding whether the State made ICWA 'active efforts.'
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading published Kansas decision applying ICWA's 'active efforts' standard and the 25 C.F.R. § 23.2 definition to a state agency's reunification work.
key_cases.quote: we do not find Mother's reluctance to participate in individual therapy meant SFM did not engage in active efforts to persuade her to do so

mandatory_reporters: Persons providing medical care or treatment: persons licensed to practice the healing arts, dentistry and optometry, persons in board-approved postgraduate training programs, licensed professional or practical nurses, and chief administrative officers of medical care facilities — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(A)

State-licensed mental health providers: psychologists, masters level psychologists, clinical psychotherapists, social workers, marriage and family therapists, clinical marriage and family therapists, behavioral analysts and assistant behavioral analysts, professional counselors, clinical professional counselors, and registered alcohol and drug abuse counselors — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(B)

Teachers, school administrators and other employees of an educational institution the child attends, and members of the board of directors, employees and officers of the Kansas State High School Activities Association — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(C)

Persons licensed by the secretary of health and environment to provide child care services, and their employees at the place where child care services are provided — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(D)

Firefighters, emergency medical services personnel, law enforcement officers, juvenile intake and assessment workers, court services officers, community corrections officers, and case managers and mediators appointed under Kan. Stat. Ann. §§ 23-3508 and 23-3502 — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(E)

Employees and volunteers of any organization, for profit or not-for-profit, that provides social services to pregnant teenagers, including counseling, adoption services and pregnancy education and maintenance — Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1)(F)
reporting_details: Kansas is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals listed in Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223(a)(1) must report, any other person who suspects a child may be a child in need of care may report but is not required to (§ 38-2223(a)(2)), and reports are made to the secretary for children and families — or to the appropriate law enforcement agency when the department is not open for business (§ 38-2223(c)(1)).

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Assignment of the report as designated on the PPS 1002, Initial Assessment (DCF PPM 1500); the 72-hour rule is stated as running from acceptance of the report and excludes weekends and state holidays (DCF PPM 1521)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in DCF PPM 1500 or 1521

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours to initiate an investigation and contact the persons who are the subject of the investigation, then 24 hours from that contact to report the status back to the referring law enforcement agency
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of a law enforcement officer's electronic referral of a child who may be a victim of abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2231(d)

A later finding is allowed only if a delay is requested by law enforcement, a county or district attorney, the court, or health or mental health professionals, or exceptional circumstances are documented in the case file (DCF PPM 2511 C.). An allowable late finding requires the Child Protection Specialist to enter "Allowable Delay" on the PPS 2011 Case Findings Section IV on or before the case finding due date; if the finding is late for a reason not allowable under PPM 2511 C., the specialist shall document with the finding: "The case finding is delayed due to a non-allowable reason per policy." (DCF PPM 2531 E.)
